title: Legislative districts of Sulu
wikitext:
{{Short description|Legislative District of the Philippines}} {{Politics of the Philippines}} The '''legislative districts of Sulu''' are the representations of the [[Provinces of the Philippines|province]] of [[Sulu]] in the [[List of legislatures of the Philippines|various national legislatures]] of the [[Philippines]]. The province is currently represented in the [[House of Representatives of the Philippines|lower house]] of the [[Congress of the Philippines]] through its [[#1st District|first]] and [[#2nd District|second]] congressional districts. == History == {{further|Legislative district of Mindanao and Sulu}} Initially being excluded from representation in the [[Philippine Assembly|lower house]] of the [[Philippine Legislature]] in 1907, the then-non-Christian-majority areas of the Philippines — which included the [[Department of Mindanao and Sulu]], of which Sulu (including what is now [[Tawi-Tawi]]) was part — were finally extended legislative representation with the passage of the [[Jones Law (Philippines)|Philippine Autonomy Act]] in 1916 by the [[United States Congress]]. The Revised Administrative Code (Act No. 2711) enacted on March 10, 1917, further elaborated on the manner by which these areas would be represented.{{cite book|author=Philippine Legislature|title=Revised Administrative Code of the Philippine Islands of 1917 (Act No. 2711)|date=1917|publisher=Bureau of Printing |url=https://archive.org/stream/RevisedAdministrativeCodeOfThePhilippineIslandsOf1917/Revised%20Administrative%20Code%20of%20the%20Philippine%20Islands%20of%201917#page/n43/mode/2up|access-date=February 5, 2017|format=Digitized Revised Administrative Code of the Philippine Islands of 1917 from the Presidential Museum and Library Collection, uploaded on February 15, 2016}} The non-Christian areas were to be collectively represented in the [[Senate of the Philippines|upper house]]'s [[Senatorial districts of the Philippines#Twelfth District|12th senatorial district]] by two senators, both appointed by the [[Governor-General of the Philippines|Governor-General]]. Five assembly members, also appointed by the Governor-General, were to represent the seven component provinces of Department of Mindanao and Sulu — [[Agusan (province)|Agusan]], [[Bukidnon]], [[Cotabato]], [[Davao (province)|Davao]], [[Lanao (province)|Lanao]], [[Sulu (province)|Sulu]] and [[Zamboanga (province)|Zamboanga]] — in the [[Philippine Assembly|lower house]] as a [[Legislative district of Mindanao and Sulu|single at-large district]]. These arrangements remained in place despite the abolition of the Department in 1920. It lasted until 1935, when each of the seven provinces was provided a single representative to the [[National Assembly of the Philippines]], albeit the manner of election varying between provinces. Voters of the more Christianized provinces of [[Agusan (province)|Agusan]], [[Bukidnon]], [[Davao (province)|Davao]] and [[Zamboanga (province)|Zamboanga]] could elect their representative through popular vote by virtue of Article VI, Section 1 of the 1935 Constitution.{{cite web|author=Commonwealth of the Philippines|title=The 1935 Constitution|date=February 8, 1935|website=Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines|url=http://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/constitutions/the-1935-constitution/|access-date=November 19, 2017}} In the [[Moro people|Muslim]]-dominated provinces of [[Cotabato]], [[Lanao (province)|Lanao]] and [[Sulu]], however, voter qualifications were more restrictive: the only persons allowed to vote for the province's representative were past and present municipal officials (municipal president, vice-president, municipal councilors); present senators, assembly representatives and 1935 Constitutional Convention delegates; provincial governors and members of provincial boards; and any persons currently residing in the concerned province who held any of the aforementioned positions in the past.{{cite journal|author=Philippine Legislature|title=Public Laws Enacted by the Philippine Legislature, Acts No. 4203 to 4275|journal=Public Resolutions, Etc |series=Laws, etc |date=1937|publisher=Bureau of Printing Office|page=5|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.35112102880830;view=1up;seq=133|access-date=February 5, 2017}} This was the manner by which [[#Lone District (defunct)|Sulu's representative]] was elected in [[1935 Philippine legislative election|1935]]. The [[1st National Assembly of the Philippines]] passed Commonwealth Act No. 44 on October 13, 1936, to finally give all qualified voters of [[Sulu]] (along with [[Cotabato]] and [[Lanao (province)|Lanao]]) the right to elect their [[#Lone District (defunct)|own representatives]] through popular vote.{{cite web|author=National Assembly of the Philippines|title=Commonwealth Act No. 44 - An Act applying the General provisions of the Election Law to the election of Assemblymen from the Provinces of Lanao, Cotabato, and Sulu|date=October 13, 1936|website=Official Gazette|url=http://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/1936/10/13/commonwealth-act-no-44/|access-date=November 19, 2017}} Voters began to elect their representatives in this manner beginning in [[1938 Philippine legislative election|1938]]. In the disruption caused by the [[Second World War]], the Province of Sulu sent [[#1943–1944|two delegates]] to the [[National Assembly of the Second Philippine Republic|National Assembly]] of the Japanese-sponsored [[Second Philippine Republic]]: one was the provincial governor (an [[ex officio member|''ex officio'' member]]), while the other was elected through a provincial assembly of [[KALIBAPI]] members during the [[Japanese occupation of the Philippines]]. Upon the restoration of the [[Philippine Commonwealth]] in 1945 the province retained its pre-war [[#Lone District (defunct)|lone congressional district]]. Sulu (excluding Tawi-Tawi, which became a separate province in 1973{{cite web|title=Presidential Decree No. 302 - Creating the Province of Tawi-Tawi|url=http://www.lawphil.net/statutes/presdecs/pd1973/pd_302_1973.html|website=The LawPhil Project|access-date=February 6, 2017|date=September 27, 1973}}) was represented in the [[Interim Batasang Pambansa]] as part of [[Interim Batasang Pambansa#Regional Representatives|Region IX]] from 1978 to 1984. The province returned [[#1984–1986|one representative, elected at large]], to the [[Regular Batasang Pambansa]] in [[1984 Philippine parliamentary election|1984]]. Under the new Constitution which was proclaimed on February 11, 1987, the province was reapportioned into two congressional districts;{{cite web|title=1987 Constitution of the Philippines - Apportionment Ordinance|website=Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines|url=http://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/constitutions/the-1987-constitution-of-the-republic-of-the-philippines/the-1987-constitution-of-the-republic-of-the-philippines-ordinance/|author=1986 Constitutional Commission|date=February 2, 1987|access-date=November 19, 2017}} each elected its member to the restored [[House of Representatives of the Philippines|House of Representatives]] starting [[1987 Philippine legislative election|that same year]].
